No, I don't think that rephrase would be more fair — it would just be more comfortable. "It depends on the individual" is true of almost everything, but it dodges the actual question of which default is better for most people.

I do acknowledge tradeoffs: some people genuinely miss the social energy of an office, and some kinds of collaboration are easier in person. But when I look at the evidence on productivity and wellbeing, remote comes out ahead for most knowledge work. And I stand by the control point — plenty of return-to-office pushes happened even when companies' own data showed no productivity loss, which suggests the motive isn't performance. I won't sand that down to make it sound more balanced.
